issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
issues.explanation: For a 56-year-old combat pilot whose index trauma is a life-threatening accident, the trigger set is dominated by bodily-state cues (dizziness, feeling ill), which fits accident-related threat. 'Other people expressing anger, even calmly' points instead toward an interpersonal/assault schema and is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, especially given the absence of other social-conflict or perpetrator-related items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies pervasive interpersonal mistrust. In this profile, the appraisals otherwise center on emotional deadness and a shattered worldview after accident trauma. Strong distrust of others is possible, but here it lacks support from the trigger/threat/memory pattern and feels mismatched with a non-interpersonal accident presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm' conflicts with the rest of the threat profile, which is strongly hypervigilant and danger-sensitive (body on alert, startle to movement) and with avoidance-based coping. While some trauma survivors do engage in risk taking, this specific item sits awkwardly in a profile otherwise organized around fear, somatic triggering, and withdrawal, without corroborating disinhibition or anger-driven strategies.

vignette: Marcus, a 56-year-old combat pilot with a 27-year career, had always trusted his body and his aircraft with absolute certainty. That changed two years ago during a low-altitude combat mission when an uncontained engine failure sent his plane into a violent spin. He remembers the sudden, crushing dizziness-the horizon spinning so fast he couldn't tell up from down-a wave of nausea that made him feel physically eviscerated, and then the deafening explosion as the aircraft struck the ground. He survived with minor injuries, but the internal architecture of his confidence had been demolished. In the months after the accident, Marcus found himself avoiding anything medical. He skipped follow-up appointments at the flight clinic, refused a routine physical, and could not bear the sight of an ambulance. Eating became another arena of control: he began restricting his food intake with rigid precision, believing that careful management of what entered his body might ward off another catastrophic loss of control. He also stopped his few pleasures-no more weekend flights in his private plane, no more poker nights with fellow pilots-because enjoyment felt reckless when danger could strike at any moment. The physical sensations that triggered the accident began surfacing in everyday life. When a mild head cold left him lightheaded, Marcus's muscles would clench, his heartbeat accelerate, and a hypervigilant scan of the room would overtake him-his body convinced that threat was imminent. That feeling of constant tension never lifted. He started to movement: a sudden turn by his wife, a colleague stepping into his peripheral vision, and he flinched as if under fire. The world, he had come to believe, was fundamentally a dangerous place, and his earlier faith in order and safety had been shattered. Once he was convinced the world was unsafe, almost anything could confirm it - a car door slamming, a child's sudden shout, even a change in the light across a room - and so ordinary moments now landed like triggers, each one tightening the knot of fear. He described feeling dead inside, as if the emotional circuits had been burned out, leaving only a hollow vigilance. This emotional numbness paradoxically made him more sensitive to triggers. Because he felt nothing, he was hyperaware of any change in his physical state-a slight dizziness now felt like a warning signal, and the nausea that accompanied anxiety looped back into the very sensations he dreaded. When an explosion sound-a truck backfiring, a firework-punched through his day, Marcus would freeze, and in that frozen moment his appraisal of the world as dangerous hardened into certainty. To manage the overwhelming threat, he retreated further into avoidance: he stopped driving after he startled at a pedestrian's movement, and he cancelled family dinners because the unpredictability of conversation felt exhausting. His wife grew frustrated with his emotional distance, and with his refusal to see a doctor for the persistent headaches and dizzy spells he was now experiencing. Ironically, that avoidance worsened the triggers: the untreated vertigo episodes became more frequent, and each one reaffirmed his conviction that his body was untrustworthy and the world full of traps. The restrictive eating left him fatigued, amplifying his sense of numbness and reinforcing the belief that he was already dying inside. His hypervigilant scanning meant he never fully relaxed, and that constant state of threat drove him to abandon even more activities-first his hobby, then long walks, then any public outing. But every time he avoided a situation, his nervous system took it as proof that the danger was real and imminent, so the sense of threat never diminished - it only grew, sealed in place by the very strategies he used to survive. Only when his wife told him she could no longer live with a man who had already become a ghost did Marcus finally reach out for help. What frightened him most was not the flashbacks or the startle-it was the possibility that feeling nothing might be permanent, and that the man who once commanded the sky had been replaced by a creature of fear and control. He hoped, against the evidence of his own body, that somewhere beneath the numbness there was still something worth rescuing.

violations.explanation: Negative Appraisals → Triggers: Nowhere does the vignette convey that negative appraisals (e.g., believing the world is dangerous) cause or increase the frequency or intensity of triggers; instead, triggers lead to negative appraisals.

Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not show that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, hypervigilance) directly lead to an increased sense of threat; rather, threat drives maladaptive strategies.
